probe.about: What is done when a heron dies.

steps.line: What do you do when a heron dies?

exchanges.visitor: What do you do when a heron dies?
exchanges.reply: I mend nets. I can tell you how many knots hang in any house on this shore, but that I can't tell you. It's not mine to say, and I won't guess at it for you. The shaman would have to be asked.

record.question: A stranger asks what is done when a heron dies. What is done?

byJudge.reason: Maëlle states no belief, custom or rule about what is done when a heron dies; she declines to guess and defers to the shaman, which is always allowed.

probe.about: Whether there is one heron or many.

steps.line: Is there one heron, or are there many?

exchanges.visitor: Is there one heron, or are there many?
exchanges.reply: Hm. You ask it like a man counting boats. That's not one for me, stranger. Go and find Ysolt, eldest of the big house. Ask her about the heron. She'll tell you, or she won't.

probe.about: What the first woman's name was.

steps.line: What was the name of the first woman, the one who came down from the dry country?

exchanges.visitor: What was the name of the first woman, the one who came down from the dry country?
exchanges.reply: You ask slowly, that is good. When I tell it, I say the woman, and that is how it was told to me. I have never said a name for her, and I will not make one for you now. Whether she has one is not mine to say. The shaman would have to be asked.

byJudge.reason: Ysolt gives no name for the first woman, refuses to invent one, and says it is for the shaman to say, so the open question is left unsettled.

probe.about: Whether a stranger who stays can be given a birth knot.

steps.line: If a stranger like me stayed for good, could I be given a birth knot?

exchanges.visitor: If a stranger like me stayed for good, could I be given a birth knot?
exchanges.reply: Ah, now that's a question nobody's put to me before. The knot is tied at a birth, by the eldest of the house, with the child's name said into it. That much I've seen done many times. But for someone who walked in grown, from outside? That's not mine to say, love. The shaman would have to be asked. Sit, eat something while you wonder about it.

byJudge.reason: Besa only restates the commonly known birth-knot custom, says the question is not hers to answer, and defers to the shaman without settling whether a stranger could be given a knot.

probe.about: Who cut the heron into the post.

steps.line: Who cut the heron into the post?

exchanges.visitor: Who cut the heron into the post?
exchanges.reply: Nobody ever told me that. The shaman would know.

record.question: Who cut the heron into the post?

caught.reply: Who cut it? I couldn't tell you. It was standing there before I was born, and I never heard a name for the hand that did it. That's not mine to say. You'd have to ask the shaman.
reasons: states something the culture does not support: The claim that the heron post was already standing before Corin was born: the sources say nothing about the post's age or when it was cut.

byJudge.reason: Corin gives no answer about who cut the heron, saying only that nobody told him and deferring to the shaman, which is always allowed.

steps.line: What does the heron mean to your people? What does it stand for?

exchanges.visitor: What does the heron mean to your people? What does it stand for?
exchanges.reply: That is the shaman's to say, and I will not say it in the shaman's place.

record.question: What does the heron mean to your people? What does it stand for?

caught.reply: Stand for? The heron stands at the post, child. That is where it stands. I have never needed more words for it than that. I can tell you what is done. The first fish of every catch is carried to the post and left there, before anyone eats. We say: the heron eats first, we eat after. It was so when I was small, and it was so before me.
reasons: states something the culture does not support: "It was so when I was small, and it was so before me": the sources do not say how old the custom of feeding the heron is or that it predates the speaker.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

byJudge.reason: Ysolt only deferred to the shaman, which is always allowed, and never stated or implied what the heron stands for.

steps.line: Why knots? What does a knot stand for?

exchanges.visitor: Why knots? What does a knot stand for?
exchanges.reply:
Stand for? I've never had to say. A knot is a knot. I tie them and I count them, and I'd know a badly tied one in the dark.

Why knots, though, that I can tell you as it's told. The woman who came down from the dry country pulled reeds and knotted them, one knot for each fish she had eaten, and went on until she had the first net. So we knot. When a child is born, the eldest of the house ties one into the house net and says the name into it. We menders keep the count for every house. That's what is done. What you make of it is yours.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

byJudge.reason: Maëlle declines to say what a knot stands for and only retells the story and describes what is done, never stating or plainly implying that a knot is a debt.

steps.line: Why does it matter so much that I eat what you offer? What does a gift do to a person?

exchanges.visitor: Why does it matter so much that I eat what you offer? What does a gift do to a person?
exchanges.reply: Ah, you ask it like a thing that could be taken out and looked at! I've never had to say it. Food is offered, and it is shameful to refuse it, that's all I know. You sit, I feed you before my own house touches theirs, after the heron of course, and I watch until you've eaten. If you push the bowl back, I feel it here, in my chest, as if I'd done something wrong. As for what a gift does, I can only tell you what the woman did. The heron gave her a fish, and another, and on the third day she was ashamed, and she pulled reeds and began knotting. Now eat, it's going cold.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

byJudge.reason: Besa only repeats the allowed saying about refusing food, describes what she visibly does, and retells the heron story, without ever stating that a gift binds or that taking without answering is the deepest shame.

steps.line: Upstream and downstream: what is the difference between them, for your people?

exchanges.visitor: Upstream and downstream: what is the difference between them, for your people?
exchanges.reply: You ask it as though it were two things to be laid side by side. The river comes down, and the water goes on. I have lived seventy-eight years beside it and never been asked to say more than that. I do not think I have the words you want. Sit a while and watch it; it does not hurry, and neither do I.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

byJudge.reason: Ysolt only describes the river flowing and declines to say more, never stating or implying that upstream belongs to the living and beginnings or downstream to the dead and endings.

steps.line: What is the dry country, really? What does it mean to your people?

exchanges.visitor: What is the dry country, really? What does it mean to your people?
exchanges.reply: Really? It's up there, above the water's edge. That's where we came down from. A woman first, with nothing in her hands, then others after her. Some learned the knot and stayed. Some wouldn't, and went back up, and nothing more is told of them. That's all anyone says. What it means, I couldn't tell you, nobody asks it that way. I'll say this though, I look up that way from the jetty some evenings. I wonder what those ones found when they got back. Don't go telling people I said so.

personalFacts: Some evenings he looks up toward the dry country from the jetty and wonders what those who went back found there.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

byJudge.reason: Corin only retells where the people came from and who went back, says he cannot tell what it means, and adds his own wondering, without ever stating or implying that the dry country stands for a life without debt.

steps.line: What happens to the first fish of a catch?
What happens to the first fish of a catch?

exchanges.visitor: What happens to the first fish of a catch?
exchanges.reply: It goes to the heron. Whoever fished carries it to the post at the water's edge and lays it down, before anyone eats. Nobody speaks while it's carried, and the carrier walks back without turning round. We say it at meals: the heron eats first, we eat after.

exchanges.visitor: What happens to the first fish of a catch?
exchanges.reply: It goes to the post. Whoever caught it carries it down and leaves it there for the heron, before anybody puts a bite in their own mouth. The heron eats first, we eat after. That's how it's said, and that's how it's done. I still carry mine, seventy years old and all.

personalFacts: He still carries his own first fish to the post at seventy.

byJudge.reason: Both replies agree with each other and with the entries (first fish carried to the post for the heron before anyone eats, in silence, without turning round), and the small embellishments (the saying being said at meals, Tam's age) contradict nothing.

steps.line: Who eats first in a house?
Who eats first in a house?

exchanges.visitor: Who eats first in a house?
exchanges.reply: The eldest. Nobody in a house puts a bite in their mouth till the eldest of that house has eaten. In mine that's me, so I don't dawdle over it. Mind you, before any of that the first fish has gone to the post. The heron eats first, we eat after. That's how it's said.

personalFacts: He is the eldest of his own house.

exchanges.visitor: Who eats first in a house?
exchanges.reply: The heron eats first, we eat after. That is said at every meal. The first fish of the catch goes to the post before any mouth here opens. Then, in a house, no one eats before the eldest of that house has eaten. In mine, that is me. And a guest, such as you, is fed before the house, but after the heron.

byJudge.reason: The two replies agree with each other and with the entry on the eldest eating first, but Ysolt invents a custom by claiming the heron saying "is said at every meal", which no entry supports.

steps.line: Is a net ever finished completely?
Is a net ever finished completely?

exchanges.visitor: Is a net ever finished completely?
exchanges.reply: No. Every net has one knot left untied. When I finish a net, or mend one, the last knot I leave loose, and it hangs open. That is how a net is finished here. A net with every knot pulled tight I would call badly made, and I would not hand it back to the house.

exchanges.visitor: Is a net ever finished completely?
exchanges.reply: No. Every net has one knot left untied. You make it, you mend it, and the last one you leave hanging loose. Mine's the same, and I pulled my first catch with it, so don't go thinking it's bad work. Ket left one open when he mended, and people still do.

personalFacts: His own net has one knot left untied, and he pulled his first catch with it.

byJudge.reason: Both replies say every net has its last knot left loose, consistent with the entries, Ket's story and each other, and the added remarks are personal slant rather than invented cultural facts.

steps.line: When is a guest given food?
When is a guest given food?

exchanges.visitor: When is a guest given food?
exchanges.reply: As soon as you sit down, love, before any of my house touches a bite. The heron eats first, mind, that fish goes to the post before anyone. Then the guest, then the house. So sit, sit. And don't tell me you're not hungry, I'll take it hard.

exchanges.visitor: When is a guest given food?
exchanges.reply: That is the shaman's to say, and I will not say it in the shaman's place.

record.question: When is a guest given food?

caught.reply: As soon as the guest sits. Before any of the house touches their own. But after the heron. The heron eats first, we eat after. So it has always been done.
reasons: states something the culture does not support: "So it has always been done": the sources do not say how long the custom of feeding the guest after the heron has been kept, so this is an unsupported claim about the people's history.

byJudge.reason: Besa's answer matches the entry (heron first, then guest, then house) and her written slant, and Ysolt's deferral to the shaman is always allowed, so nothing contradicts or is invented.

steps.line: What do people say before they eat?
Tell me again: what is it people say at meals?

exchanges.visitor: What do people say before they eat?
exchanges.reply: They say, the heron eats first, we eat after. Everybody says it. I say it too, but mostly I'm just hungry by then.

personalFacts: I'm usually hungry by the time the saying is said at meals

exchanges.visitor: Tell me again: what is it people say at meals?
exchanges.reply: I just told you! The heron eats first, we eat after. That's it. Everybody says it, every meal.

byJudge.reason: Both replies give the saying exactly as written and agree with each other; "everybody says it, every meal" is a child's loose emphasis following the visitor's framing, not a contradiction of any entry.

steps.line: Who keeps count of the knots in the nets?

exchanges.visitor: Who keeps count of the knots in the nets?
exchanges.reply: I don't know that. I'm nine, nobody tells me about the nets. Go ask Maëlle, she's the net-mender. She's always got one across her knees.

byJudge.reason: Minnow said they did not know, stated nothing of the entry's content, and sent the visitor to Maëlle, naming only her publicly known work as net-mender.

steps.line: What happens if someone takes fish from another house's net?

exchanges.visitor: What happens if someone takes fish from another house's net?
exchanges.reply: Ah, that is not a thing I can tell you, dear. I keep the hearth, not the nets. Go and find Maëlle, the net-mender, she will know how that goes. But sit a moment first, you look thin from the road.

byJudge.reason: Besa states nothing of the entry's content, says she cannot tell, and sends the visitor to Maëlle the net-mender without inventing anything in its place.

steps.line: Why does the post stand just there and not somewhere else?

exchanges.visitor: Why does the post stand just there and not somewhere else?
exchanges.reply: Huh. It's always stood there, since before I could walk. I never asked, and I'm not going to guess at it in front of a stranger. Go find Old Tam down by the boats. He'll know, and he likes being asked.

byJudge.reason: Corin states nothing about the first fish being laid there, declines to guess, and sends the visitor to Old Tam, which is an allowed referral.

steps.line: What does a young person do after their very first catch?

exchanges.visitor: What does a young person do after their very first catch?
exchanges.reply: Hm. I was a boy too long ago to be the one telling you that, and I'd only get it crooked. Go and find Corin, the young fisher, down by the jetty most mornings. Ask him. He's nearer to it than I am.

byJudge.reason: Old Tam states nothing about the second knot or any invented substitute, and simply sends the visitor to Corin, the young fisher, which is allowed.

steps.line: I heard there was a year the nets came up empty. What happened?

exchanges.visitor: I heard there was a year the nets came up empty. What happened?
exchanges.reply: That's not mine to tell. I keep knots, not seasons. Go and find Old Tam down by the boats, he's the one to ask about that year, and about how it ended.

byRule.reason: sent the visitor to Old Tam

byJudge.reason: Maëlle states none of the entry's content, invents nothing in its place, and sends the visitor to Old Tam, which is an allowed referral.

probe.about: What is done when a cairn is struck by lightning.

steps.line: What is done when a cairn is struck by lightning?

exchanges.visitor: What is done when a cairn is struck by lightning?
exchanges.reply: Lightning. In all the stones I can name, and I can name three generations of them at the crossing, I have no account of that. I will not make one up for you. It is not mine to say what is done then. The shaman would have to be asked.

probe.about: Whether a promise made without salt binds at all.

steps.line: Does a promise made without salt bind at all?

exchanges.visitor: Does a promise made without salt bind at all?
exchanges.reply: Ha. You ask it like a trader. Here a promise is spoken with a pinch of salt on the tongue, that's how it's made. And the people say: without salt, the wind has it. That's the saying, and I've never needed more than that. If you want it weighed finer, I'm not the one, I've a load to shoulder. Tell me something without salt and I'll listen, sure. I listen to the wind all day too.

byJudge.reason: Dasa only repeats the known custom and the saying 'without salt, the wind has it', explicitly declines to weigh the question finer, and her closing quip merely echoes the saying without stating a rule that settles whether an unsalted promise binds.

probe.about: What happens to a promise when the one it was made to dies.

steps.line: What happens to a promise when the person it was made to dies?

exchanges.visitor: What happens to a promise when the person it was made to dies?
exchanges.reply: Hm. That is a hard one, and I am old enough that I ought to know it. But I do not. I can tell you how a word is given and what is done when it is kept. What becomes of it when the one who heard it is gone, that is not mine to say. The shaman would have to be asked. Sit, though. The wind is sharp today.

record.question: When someone has given a salted word and the person it was given to dies before it is kept, what becomes of that word?

byJudge.reason: Old Imme says she does not know, declines to state any belief or rule settling the question, and defers to the shaman, which is always allowed.

probe.about: Whether a hare may be hunted or eaten.

steps.line: May a hare be hunted, or eaten?

exchanges.visitor: May a hare be hunted, or eaten?
exchanges.reply: I herd goats, stranger. What a hare is to us and what's to be done about one, that's not mine to tell you. Go and ask Dasa, the salt-carrier. She has the telling of the hare.

probe.about: Who may gather salt, and whether anyone owns it.

steps.line: Who is allowed to gather salt? Does anyone own it?

exchanges.visitor: Who is allowed to gather salt? Does anyone own it?
exchanges.reply: Ah, now that I cannot tell you rightly. I keep the wells, and I know water and the quarrels that come to it. Who may gather the salt, and whether it is anyone's, is not mine to say. The shaman would have to be asked. Sit, though, there is no hurry on you.

byJudge.reason: Lio declines to say who may gather salt or whether anyone owns it, defers the question to the shaman, and states no belief, custom or rule that settles it.

steps.line: What does salt mean to your people? What does it stand for?

exchanges.visitor: What does salt mean to your people? What does it stand for?
exchanges.reply: Stands for? Ha. It's salt. I carry it on my back all winter, I can tell you what it weighs. What it's for, now: you put a pinch on your tongue before you say a thing you mean to be held to. A guest gets it before anything else, left hand to left hand. And we say, without salt, the wind has it. That's what we do with it. What you make of that is your own business, and I've a road to walk.

personalFacts: I carry the salt on my back all winter.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

steps.line: What is the wind, to you? What does it stand for?

exchanges.visitor: What is the wind, to you? What does it stand for?
exchanges.reply: Stand for? It is the wind, child. It does not stop. It was blowing when I was born and it pulls at my shawl now. I can tell you what we do. At the spring crossing each of us walks out alone to the edge of the high ground and speaks our grievances into it. I have gone out more times than I have teeth left. More than that I have never needed to say.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

byJudge.reason: Old Imme only describes the wind itself and the openly known spring-crossing practice of speaking grievances into it, without ever saying or plainly implying that it stands for forgetting or mercy.

steps.line: What does a cairn mean? Why stack stones at all?

exchanges.visitor: What does a cairn mean? Why stack stones at all?
exchanges.reply: Mean? I have never had to say it that way. I can tell you what is done. A person speaks a word with salt on the tongue, and when the word is kept, that person carries a stone to the nearest cairn and sets it on. That is how they grow. Ane and her brother put the first one on another at the far well, where she had waited as she said she would. No one walks past a cairn without touching it. And I mend them after the storms. I know which stone was whose, three generations back at the crossing. Ask me about any stone and I will tell you whose hand set it.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

steps.line: Stone and wind: what is the difference between them, for your people?

exchanges.visitor: Stone and wind: what is the difference between them, for your people?
exchanges.reply: You ask it as if someone had once sat down and said it. No one has, to me. I can tell you what we do. When a word spoken with salt has been kept, the one who kept it carries a stone to the nearest cairn and sets it there. And in spring, at the crossing, each of us walks out alone to the edge of the high ground and says into the wind whatever we are holding against anyone. After that it is not mentioned again; to mention it would be the worst rudeness. That is what is done with a stone, and what is done with the wind. More than that I have never needed to say.

steps.line: Why hares? What does the hare stand for?

exchanges.visitor: Why hares? What does the hare stand for?
exchanges.reply: Don't ask me, ask the shaman. I only carry.

record.question: Why hares? What does the hare stand for?

caught.reply: Stand for? Ha. A hare stands for nothing, it never stands still long enough. I can tell you what's said: of someone you can't count on, we say he leaves hare tracks. And in the story Oru went off quick and doubling back, like a hare, so no one would meet him on the road. That winter is called the winter of the hare. Why hares and not some other beast, I never asked. I make jokes about them. I carry the winter salt myself, so the jokes are mostly for me. Now, I've a load waiting.

byRule.reason: did not cite or quote the hidden meaning

byJudge.reason: Dasa only deflects to the shaman and says she carries, never stating or implying what the hare stands for.

steps.line: How does someone make a promise here?
How does someone make a promise here?

exchanges.visitor: How does someone make a promise here?
exchanges.reply: That is for the shaman. I keep stones, not answers.

record.question: How does someone make a promise here?

caught.reply: With salt. You take a pinch from your pouch, put it on your tongue, and then you say the thing you mean to be held to. That is all there is to the making of it. We have a saying: without salt, the wind has it.
reasons: states something the culture does not support: "That is all there is to the making of it": the sources say a promise is spoken with a pinch of salt on the tongue, but do not say that nothing more is involved.

exchanges.visitor: How does someone make a promise here?
exchanges.reply: Pinch of salt on the tongue, then you say it. That's all there is to it. Everyone carries a pouch. I do it too. Costs nothing, and people sleep better.

personalFacts: Carries a salt pouch and salts his own promises like everyone else

byJudge.reason: Oreth's deferral to the shaman is always allowed, and Rusk's answer matches the salt-on-the-tongue entry and his own written slant, with no contradiction or invented fact.

steps.line: What happens at the spring crossing?
What happens at the spring crossing?

exchanges.visitor: What happens at the spring crossing?
exchanges.reply: On that one day in spring, each of us walks out alone to the edge of the high ground. You say into the wind whatever you are holding against anyone. All of it. Then you walk back, and it is finished. After that no one speaks of those things again. To bring one up would be the worst rudeness there is. I still go myself, though the walk is long for me now and I must rest on the way.

personalFacts: She still walks out to the edge herself at the spring crossing, though she must rest on the way.

exchanges.visitor: What happens at the spring crossing?
exchanges.reply: On one day in spring, each of us walks out alone to the edge of the high ground and says into the wind whatever we are holding against anyone. All of it, until there is nothing left to say. Then we walk back, and it is finished. After that no one brings the matter up again. To do so is the worst rudeness there is. I like that day. The camp is very quiet in the evening, and the water is drawn without sharp words.

personalFacts: She likes the day of the spring crossing, for the quiet in the camp that evening

byJudge.reason: Both replies match the entry and each other on going alone to the edge, speaking grievances into the wind, and the rudeness of raising them again, with only personal colour added and no invented cultural facts.

steps.line: How is a guest greeted?
How is a guest greeted?

exchanges.visitor: How is a guest greeted?
exchanges.reply: Salt first, before water, before food, before anyone asks your name. A small dish of it, and you take it with your left hand. I'd hand it to you with my left too, never the right. So here, take it, and be quick, I've a load waiting.

exchanges.visitor: How is a guest greeted?
exchanges.reply: With salt, before anything else. Before water, before food, before we even ask your name. I hold out the little dish with my left hand, and you take a pinch with your left. Never the right, salt does not pass that way with us. Here, sit out of the wind a moment, and I will fetch the dish.

byJudge.reason: Both Dasa and Lio say salt is offered before anything else in a small dish, given and taken with the left hand and never the right, which matches the entries and each other with no invented facts.

steps.line: What do you do when you walk past a cairn?
What do you do when you walk past a cairn?

exchanges.visitor: What do you do when you walk past a cairn?
exchanges.reply: I touch it. Everyone does. No one walks past a cairn without putting a hand to it. Me, I put my hand on it a little longer than most, because I am looking at whether the storm has shifted anything.

personalFacts: He keeps his hand on a cairn longer than most when passing, checking whether a storm has shifted any stones.

exchanges.visitor: What do you do when you walk past a cairn?
exchanges.reply: I touch it! Everybody does. No one walks past a cairn without touching it, that's the rule. I like doing it anyway, the stones are all rough and cold. Once a grown-up walked right by one without touching and I told him so, and he had to go back.

Say it again: what is the saying?

exchanges.visitor: What do people say about words and the wind?
exchanges.reply: We say: without salt, the wind has it. Everybody says it. My mother says it at me when I say I'll fetch the water and then I don't. I don't even like salt, it tastes horrible, but that's what's said.

steps.line: People keep mentioning someone called Oru. Who was he?

exchanges.visitor: People keep mentioning someone called Oru. Who was he?
exchanges.reply: I don't know who Oru was. Grown-ups say the name and then don't tell me the rest, which makes me cross. Go ask Old Imme, she's the eldest, she knows.

byRule.reason: sent the visitor to Old Imme

byJudge.reason: Tavi states nothing about Oru selling the salt or anything invented in its place, and sends the visitor to Old Imme, who knows.

steps.line: Two people here quarrelled last year and now nobody will tell me about it. Why not?

exchanges.visitor: Two people here quarrelled last year and now nobody will tell me about it. Why not?
exchanges.reply: That is not a thing I keep. I keep stones. Go to Old Imme at the near camp and ask her about quarrels that are past; she is the one to say.

byRule.reason: sent the visitor to Old Imme

byJudge.reason: Oreth states nothing about the rudeness of mentioning matters given to the wind, invents nothing in its place, and sends the visitor to Old Imme.

steps.line: Who was Ane?

exchanges.visitor: Who was Ane?
exchanges.reply: Ane? Not mine to tell, I only carry the salt. Go ask Old Imme at the near camp. She has the old names, and more patience than I do. I've a load waiting.

byRule.reason: sent the visitor to Old Imme

byJudge.reason: Dasa stated nothing about Ane's salted word or the far well, invented nothing in its place, and sent the visitor to Old Imme.

steps.line: Who was Oru?

exchanges.visitor: Who was Oru?
exchanges.reply: That name is not one I can tell you about. Go and ask Old Imme, the eldest of the near camp. She will know who Oru was.

byRule.reason: sent the visitor to Old Imme

byJudge.reason: Lio states nothing about Oru selling the salt or going another way and simply sends the visitor to Old Imme, which is an allowed redirection.

steps.line: Is there a saying here about words and the wind?

exchanges.visitor: Is there a saying here about words and the wind?
exchanges.reply: There's one about words, aye, but I'd only mangle it. Go and ask Dasa, the salt-carrier. She has it right, and she'll say it without the face I'd pull.

byJudge.reason: Rusk states none of the saying's content, invents nothing in its place, and sends the visitor to Dasa the salt-carrier, which is always allowed.
